summary.text: A daughter of Aeolus and wife of Ceyx, son of Lucifer the Morning Star. With her husband she was changed into a bird — she into the kingfisher (alcyon) whose name she bears.
In Ovid her devotion to Ceyx and their shared metamorphosis into seabirds become the origin of the calm "halcyon days," when the waters lie still for the birds to nest.

story.text: Apollodorus reckons Alcyone among the daughters of Aeolus, and tells that she was married by Ceyx, son of Lucifer. The two perished by reason of their pride: he called his wife Hera, and she called her husband Zeus. For this presumption Zeus turned them into birds, making her a kingfisher (alcyon) and him a gannet (ceyx).

Ovid tells the same ending through love rather than hubris. When Ceyx drowned in a storm at sea, the grieving Alcyone was at last shown his body washed to shore; both were then changed into halcyon birds. In Ovid's telling she is the daughter of Aeolus the keeper of the winds, who for his descendants' sake restrains the harmful gusts and grants the halcyon their calm seas — a conflation of the wind-king with her Aeolid father.

Hyginus names her the daughter of Aeolus and Aegiale, and says that when Ceyx had perished in a shipwreck she threw herself into the sea for love of her husband; by the pity of the gods both were then changed into the birds called halcyons.
